title: The whole body
hookLine: steps three and four: sensing the whole body, calming it
last: LONG AND SHORT — JUST KNOW IT.

lines: A BAG YOU FORGOT YOU'RE HOLDING.
FEEL ALL OF IT. LET IT SETTLE.
cards: Right now, without moving, notice your shoulders. Are they up near your ears? Now your jaw.
Is it clenched? Your forehead. Your hands.

Is any of them holding on for no reason at all? It's easy to carry a body around all day like a bag you've forgotten you're holding. Steps three and four of the breathing discourse bring the body back into the picture.
First, feel all of it. Then, let it settle.

teach.b: Notice a small shift in the words. Steps one and two said: a person knows. Steps three and four say: a person trains.

teach.h: THE WHOLE BREATH, OR THE WHOLE BODY?
teach.b: Experiencing the whole body, I will breathe in; experiencing the whole body, I will breathe out.
Then: calming the body's activity, I will breathe in and out. Knowing has become training; something is being gently developed now. But what does the whole body mean?
Here Buddhists read the text differently, and it's worth knowing both.
The Visuddhimagga, the old manual, says it's the body of the breath: you feel each breath from its beginning, through its middle, to its end, the whole length of it, not just the tip.

Some modern teachers read it as the physical body: the breath felt everywhere, chest, belly, back, shoulders, the whole body breathing. Both readings are practiced today, and the text itself doesn't settle it.

Then step four: calming. In a related discourse, the body's activity is explained as the breath itself. So as you feel the whole body, the breath naturally softens and slows, and the body goes quiet with it.
You create the conditions, and the settling happens, like mud sinking to the bottom of a still glass of water.
The shoulders come down. The jaw lets go.

how: In Buddhist breath meditation, practitioners move from simply knowing the breath to feeling it through its whole length, or through the whole body, and letting the body grow calm.

o: a calm state reached after meditating
the body, felt whole as you breathe
the mind that watches the breath

games.q: what's inside the steps — tap the pairs.
p: the whole body of the breath

s: from step three the text says a person trains
knowing becomes training: I will breathe in, I will breathe out.
all Buddhists agree on what the whole body means
the old manual reads it as the whole breath; some modern teachers read it as the physical body.

you create the conditions, and the settling happens, like mud sinking in still water.

games.q: you're told to feel the whole body while breathing. which reading does the old manual give?
o: the whole breath, beginning, middle and end.
only the tip of the nose.
games.why: the Visuddhimagga reads it as the whole body of the breath. some modern teachers read it as the physical body, and both are practiced.

practice: Find the breath, then widen your attention until you feel each one from its very beginning to its very end, and wider still, moving the belly, the chest, the back, the shoulders.
On each out-breath, let one place soften: the jaw, then the shoulders, then the hands. Don't force the calm; let the body find its own stillness, breath by breath.

wordCard.voice: Kaya. Body: steps three and four of the breathing discourse, feeling the whole breath, or the whole body, and letting it calm.

orig.note: Pali: body, and also a group or collection; which body is meant here is debated.

carryVoice: Your line: the body settles. Steps three and four bring it back into the picture. That's day one hundred and nine.
